PREFACE
The plan of this edition conforms, in general, with the estab-
lished tradition of the New VARIORuM series, and is described
in the following section. The proportions of the various edi-
torial parts, however, are governed by the peculiarities of the
play.
Troilus and Cressida has been seldom acted.Therefore,in
the section of the Aopendix dealing with modern productions
of the play, rather more details than usual are given as to the
staging and the casting. No performances have been dis-
covered except in England, Germany, France, Austria, Hun-
gary, Czechoslovakia, and the United States; but the closing of
foreign sources of information by the war has precluded an
exhaustive inquiry into European productions. Some instances
many.
The play has aroused a good deal of critical interest, chiefy
on the grounds of its purpose and general meaning. It has been
the occasion of so many varied and conflicting interpretations
that it has been thought necessary to deal with them in several
sections of the Appendix. Comments will be found there which
ordinarily would go into the section on General Criticism. The
text, on the other hand, has received from critics a more per-
functory treatment,both in the adjudicating between Quarto
and Folio and in the commentary. This fact indicates that
the play has provoked less interest in its details than in its
intention.
The present edition is the first to give full collation of all the
known Quartos and of the first printing of the first page in the
Folio.The problems of the two basic texts (Quarto and Folio),
although they are nowhere very serious for an understanding of
    e     
rather full treatment.
My work has been carried on,in small part at the Huntington
and Folger Shakespeare Libraries, but mostly at the Library of
the University of Illinois.The editor is deeply obligated to
Dean R.D.Carmichael and the Graduate Research Board of
the University for material grants in aid; to various graduate
students who have helped him in assembling and checking ma.

Professor Hillebrand had presented the body of his completed
manuscript of 1943 to the late Dr. Joseph Quincy Adams, at
that time General Editor, who penciled various suggestions
upon it. These suggestions I have tried to observe, usually
quoting his note with an A attached to distinguish it. The
present General Editor, Professor Hyder Edward Rollins, has
given of his time and advice far more than is called for by his
office,thoughhis contributions arenot of such a nature that
one can attach a symbol to them. He has, in fact, been co-
editor as well as General Editor; and his work has been of basic
importance.
I have checked ProfessorHillebrand's manuscript to originals
in detail,as he would have done, silently inserting references
wherever needed. The text of the first printing of the first page
of Troilus in the^first folio has been checked to a photostat of
the copy in the Folger Shakespeare Library which Dr. J. G.
McManaway identifies as Copy 2. The remainder of the text
has been checked to the Ernest Ingoid copy of the first folio in
the University of Illinois Library. Of the other works used,
except the originals of the quartos, only a very few are not in
our library.
I have not in any way altered materially the content of Pro-
fessor Hillebrand's work,and have indicated all inserts of con-
sequence. I have supplemented his work down to June 30,
1949, since in a work of this nature some terminal date had to
be set. I have managed, however, to insert briefy the im-
portant technical discoveries between that date and publica-
tion, though I could not, of course, digest all· materials printed
while the work was in press. My inserts are marked with a B.
Basically, the style of the original manuscript has been fol-

PREFACE
vii
lowed, but with some changes toward conformity with recent
volumes in the series,where that did notinvolve the risk of
confusing the content.Itis hoped that the end resultwill be
accurate as to fact and intelligible as to form. Naturally, I
have compiled and added such mechanical aids as theList of
Abbreviations and so forth, since the original manuscript con-
tained only the body of the work.
The Research Board of the University of Illinois has been
very generous in supplying me with all possible assistance, as
usual;and those who aidedProfessorHillebrandhavecontinued
their kindness to me. I am sure I can speak for all who have
lent a hand and say that we hope the work is now finally in
print approximately as Professor Hillebrand himself would have
completed it.
T.W.BALDWIN
July 15, 1952

THE PLAN OF THE WORK
This edition follows the plan ofits predecessors in the New
VARIoRuM series. On the same page with the basic text, which
in this case is that of the First Folio, are given the significant
variant readings of the'Quarto,of the three later folios,and of a
selected list of editions from Rowe to Kittredge, together with
such Commentary on the text as the editor has thought worthy
of inclusion, not only for the purpose of explaining the text but
at times as illustrations of the history of Shakespearean criti-
cism. In the Appendix are gathered such discussions of date,
textual provenance, source, general purpose or meaning of the
play, stage history, and criticism as fall outside the field of
specific textual commentary.
The text of the First Folio has been chosen because,on the
whole,it seems tobe later than thatof theQuarto and because
it is less carelessly printed.But the relationship between
Quarto and Folio is complex, as the discussion in the Appendix
shows, and the balance of authority between them is fairly
even.* In the few cases where the Quarto has passages which
are omitted from the Folio, those passages are included and are
marked by square brackets.
is meant every variation which, in the opinion of the editor,
may be of interest to the scholar. Thus are includea not only
the differences of language and pointing which must necessarily
be considered in forming the modern text,but such instances of
errorand such variations of spelling as exhibit what may be
called the printing house (or perhaps scribal) character of the
Quarto. Because there is only one quarto for this play, and
because the text of this quarto is of considerable independence,
it has been thought desirable to make a pretty full collation.
But hundreds of minor variations of no textual significance,
such as the placing of colons and question marks at the ends of
speeches where in current punctuation periods ought to be, are
not included. Likewise the three later folios are fully col-
lated, even to the inclusion of a few obvious mistakes.
*Recent findings lean toward Q as the “substantive,"or rather the more
substantive,text.Even so,however,because of the peculiarrelationships be

THEPLANOFTHEWORK
For the selected modern editions,from Rowe on,the principle
is to include everything pertinent to the meaning of the text
and in general to its metrical"feeling,'except for those changes
due to modernization of spelling and punctuation which are
of then to than, of Ile to I'll, of I to ay, or (unless the sense is
affected) of the question mark to the exclamation mark.Nor
are the very numerous elisions of syllables which appear in
modern editions included unless they mark a real difference of
speaking (e.g. that's for that is, 1.ii.156) and not a mere slurring
(such as gen'ral for general). On the other hand, care is taken
to present every instance of a modern expansion of an elision
in the basic text (as finest for fin'st, 1.i.352); likewise to present
all instances where the modern practice of elision seems to differ
from the Elizabethan (as in remembred, Q, Fi, remember'd, Pope,
rememb'red, Kittredge—I1.iii.25).
Itwouldnotbepracticableor usefultolist all thevariations
of punctuation which occur in modern texts and which are due
in large part to changes of custom and to individual habit. It
is rarely important to know whether a colon or a semicolon is
used,whether parentheses or commas,whether an exclamation
point or a period; nor is it requisite to note the obvious, such
as the insertion of commas setting off vocatives or of apostrophes
to mark the possessive.The general principle has been to in-
clude everything which bears on the grouping of words and the
interpretation of the text, without differentiating minutiae oi
editorialpractice.
Besides variants the Textual Notes also contain all the con-
jectural emendations, or nearly all, which have been found,
whether or not theyhavebeen adopted into anyof thetexts.
In comparison with other Shakespearean plays Troilus and
Cressida has been given relatively few textual conjectures, and
accordingly it has been thought best to be generous in listing
them. In some few cases the present editor has revolted, and
his gorge has risen at some which he has included out of defer-
ence to custom, like Keightley's expansions of what he thought
to be defectivelines.
One can after all justify these as instances
of critical aberration and warnings to future editors. When an
editor has adopted the conjecture of another man, that fact is
indicated in this manner: Warburton (Theobald conj.).But
when an editor inserts his own conjecture,the emendation is

THEPLANOFTHEWORK
xili
treated as a textual variant and dated from its first appearance in
the text.
In the selection of modern texts I have been guided in general
by the selections in previous volumes of the New Variorum, but
also by the principle that editions should be admitted only
when they make significant contributions to the history of the
text.Thus no distinction is made between the two variants
of Rowe which are dated r7og* or between the two variants of
Johnson which are dated 176s.f Of editions which have ap
peared in these lists before, I have rejected the so-called third
and fourth editions of Theobald (1752, 1762) because they
appeared after Theobald's death and have no known authority
(although I have included two or three readings from each on
occasion), and also the ambitious Works of Shakespeare by J. O.
Halliwell in sixteen volumes, 1853-64. This monumental edi-
tion, however valuable for its commentary and illustrations, has
a negligible text, at least for Troilus and Cressida.It should be
admitted that on the test of significant contributions one might
exclude the so-called Variorum of 18r3, the second Knight
edition, the third Dyce,and the second Cambridge, but these
have become habitues in the New Variorum.

In the Textual Notes the hyphen (as in Rowe-Johns.) indi-
cates the agreement of all intervening texts with the first and
last named.Unless exception is made it also indicates agree-
ment of all editions by any one of the editors so included. (In
the given example it would include Han.ii.)
Coll. MS. refers to Collier's copy of the Second Folio, bearing
manuscript annotations supposedly of the seventeenth century.
Singer MS. refers to a similar Folio, of undoubted authenticity,
once in the possession of S. W. Singer.t Long MS. refers to a
copy of the Second Folio at Pembroke College, Cambridge, con-
taining marginal emendations by Theobald, Warburton, and
some other (unidentified) persons. It was used by the Cam-
bridge editors↑ and citations are from that source.The List
of Abbreviations and Symbols will explain the remainder.
References to acts, scenes, and lines of Troilus and Cressida
arefrom thepresent text.Citations ofallother Shakespearean
plays follow the second Cambridge text (18g1-3). Where such
citations occur in passages quoted from editors and com-
mentators, they are also usually silently changed to conform
with this text.

35. So ... thence] TEisELTON (N.Q., 3 June, 1899, P. 423): [There is a material
difference between the F reading and the modern.See Textual Notes.] The
modern version makes Troilus accuse himself of treachery towards himself on
the ground that it is not really true that Cressida is ever absent from his
thoughts; the original makes him accuse himself of treachery towards Cressida,
since,onhis own admission, shemust beat times absent fromhis thoughts,orit
could not be said she came into them.As the latter is,I submit,the more
natural position for a youthful lover, like Troilus, to take, I would certainly
advocateareversion to the original text.--PoRTER and CLARKE(ed.1gro):
Rowe's change .. is like other modern improvements, not very suitable to the
original structure.Troylus is complaining, not that she is never absent from
his thoughts,but that.she is really thence, bodily away from him, present in
his thoughts only.Pandarus interrupts him, while he was going on to say how
vividly her presence came in his mind only to torment and tantalize him.-
TATLoCK (ed.1912) and PARADIsE (ed.1927) are exceptional among editors in
keeping the Folio reading.PARADIsE thus explains:“Troilus,breaking off his
original train of thought, calls himself a traitor for admitting that Cressida is
ever absent from his thoughts and says that when she is absentfor a moment
she instantly returns."[The“then-when”rhetorical device is conclusive for
theauthoritativereading.-B.]

14. feuen yeares fiege] HERTzBERG (ed.r877): That Shakespeare's chronol-
ogy does not agree with the Homeric, is to be expected; but he has also per-
mitted himself material variations from his medieval sources, for dramatic
purposes. It is true that according to Le Fevre the death of Hector falls in the
"seventh year"of the war.But also according to him Patroclus is killed by
Hectorearlyin the siege..andAchilles'inactionfromlove ofPolyxena first
begins in the year after Hector's death. .. Of the leading motif of the Iliad,
the “wrath of Achilles" for the rape of Briseis, Dares knew as little as his
followers and Shakespeare, himself. As to the vain attempt of Agamem.
non, Nestor, and Ulysses to rouse Achilles from his apathy, there is, to be sure,
much said from Benoit and Guido on. But the attendant intrigue,the ex-
citation of Achilles' jealousy by ostensibly favoring Ajax,—-is Shakespeare's
own invention.

60. Vlyffes] Lewis (Lion and the Fox, [rg27], p. 212): In a play like Troilus
and Cressida the weakness of the grand style and of blank verse becomes pe-
culiarly apparent. .. It transfigures everything at once. monotonously
heightening it, so that it is impossible, in the midst of its splendours, to convey
anythingbut the mostelevated and dazzlingperfections.
W'ith Ulysses,
for example, the intention is to convey a feeling of craft and“policy'; and you
would expect his utterance to be correspondingly circumspect, rather insinuat-
ing than grand. You would not expect organ notes to issue from his mouth as
you would were it the mouth of Roland or Renaud.Yet...the moment he
            sn
speak more grandly.

strange.He is a scold, quick of tongue and coward of heart,and in Hamlet's
phrase “must fall a cursing, like a very drab."He stings and buzzes about
the unwieldy Ajax,and the latter expresses his contempt for mere cleverness,
by retorting, You are not a man at all, you are only a shrill-tongued shrew.-
DEIGHToN (ed. 1go6) takes the phrase as a taunt at Thersites' cowardice,
noting that in Aeschylus' Agamemnon,line 1625, the Chorus addresses
the chiefs“Greekish girls."

99. Enter Caffandra] KNIGHT (ed. 1841, p. 143): One of the most extraordi-
nary subtleties of Shakspere's Troilus and Cressida arises out of the circum-
stance that the real heroic tragedyis found side by side with the ironical heroic.
Cassandra, short as the character is, may be classed among the finest creations
of art.Dryden omits Cassandra altogether.Was this a want of real percep-
tion of “the grounds" of tragedy; or an instinct which avoided the higher
heroic,when it would come into contrast withhis own feebler conceptions?
passions, the worldliness, which are everywhere around her. The solemn and
the earnest arein alliancewith madness.[Thelament ofCassandra occursin
Lydgate and Caxtonin connection with the debatewhichprecedes the expedi-
tion of Paris to the court of Menelaus (see first note on this scene).But it is
placedaftertheconclusionofthedebate,whenthenewsofthedecisionreaches
her. Sh. has given a more dramatic turn by plunging her into the conference,
at the same time strengthening the impression that theTrojans are stubbornly
bent on their own destruction.-—ED.]

(v1; 2) defines “to blame, reproach, reprove; to revile, scold."For the six-
teenth and seventeenth centuries it lists no use, in this sense,in the active
voice,and perhaps the active use was old-fashioned by 16oo.Nevertheless

105-1o6. The Elephant, etc.]Aristotle had occasion to deny the vulgar error
that elephants have no knees, and sleep standing up.See Hist.animalium
(ed.Smith and Ross, 1912), 498* 8, and De incessu animalium, 7og* 10.It is
curious that against his great authority the error continued to be current, so
that Sir Thomas Browne felt it necessary to give a chapter (Bk IIl, ch. 1) of
his Pseudodoxia to its exposure. The editor is obliged to his colleague, Pro
fessor T.W.Baldwin,for calling attention to a proverb of Carolus Bovillus
(included with the Adagia of Erasmus in sixteenth century editions;e.g.I574;
Basiliae, Pt. II, p. 614): “Homo genibus elephantinis."The explication runs:
"De superbo,qui uix Deum, ne dicam hominem ullo honore, ne aperti capitis
aut genu flexi, afficere dignetur. Elephanti genua non plicant, neque se in-
curuant. Vnde cadentes surrigere se nequeunt: ab homine erigi debent."
Mr.Baldwin informs me that “this adage is retained in the Epitome of the
larger work by Victor Giselinus, which had considerable currency in the gram
mar schools."The application of the unkneeling elephant to the haughty
much older than Sh.Perhapsit'may have contributed to theperseverance
of the error.

I5. ftate of Grace} WILsoN (Christian Dictionary, 1622 ed., defines “grace”"
as “The bountifull liberality of God, enabling vs to giue to the poore, 2 Cor.
9, 8."" Geneva (r579) reads, "And God is able to make all grace to abound
should giue but litle,distrusting to impouerishe them selues thereby,he sheweth
that Godwilsoblesse theirliberall heartes,thatboth they shal haueinough for
may do good & helpe others at all times."The Servant asks if Pandarus is in
this state of grace; i.e., if he is going to give a gratuity; but Pandarus replies
as if “Grace' were the title of honor, saying he is only a lord; i.e., that he has
no gratuity to give. NoBLE (Sh's Biblical Knowledge, 1935, Pp. 214-is)
comments, “This servant is, as anybody can understand, playing on the cant
phrases of fervent devotees, and the point wouid lose nothing in gesture and
tone of voice.‘You are in the state of grace'after'I do desire it'(taken by the
Servant to be a desire that his honour.might be better) addressed to the dis-
and lordship are my titles.'The ridicule of the cant phrases of zealots in
Twelfth Night, 1.v.120-21, and Othello,11.i.94 ff., should be compared with this
passage here." I am not certain that any ridicule of cant phrases is intended,
only comical, punning parody.——-B.

7.walke off] At a distance, out of ear-shot. As a matter of fact, the actor
wouldwalkoff stage,andbothinstances of thephrase citedbyN.E.D.under

Elysium, the abode of the blest, is described in Aen. 6. 037-659. Most of
Shakespeare's references are without significance,Elysium being equivalent to
Paradise. Of more significance, however, are Troil. [Il1.ii.r3], Ant. [rv.iv.
50-S4l, and Cymb. [v.iv.97-98]. In Ant. we read: Stay for me: Where souls
do couch on flowers, we'll haua in hand. .. Again in Cymb.: Poor shadows
of Elysium, hence, and rest Upon your never-withering banks of fowers. In
each case, then,where Elysium is described the fowers are given chief promi-
nence. Now Vergil, though mentioning ‘the smiling lawns of happy groves'
and‘the fragrant bay-trees,'and saying that the ghosts‘dwell in the shady
woods,and haunt thecouches thattheriver-banksafford,andthemeadows
that thefountainsfreshen,'does notmention any flowers;butin theHomeric
Hades the spirits pass ‘along the mead of asphodel,' Od. I1. 539, and the
asphodel is a species of lily. (In Aen. 6. 883 Anchises says 'give me handfuls of
lilies,' which implies that they grew in Vergil's Elysian Fields also).[Sh.'s
contemporaries knew of the asphodel,and their dictionaries identified it

my welbeioued is mine, who feedeth among the lilies.Troilus degrades this

offowers.Incidentally,this genesis of thefigure and therelationship ofthe

1g f.I am giddy, etc.] ARTHUR SyMONs (Harper's Mag., CxV, 19o7, 662): In
Troilus we get the sensual man, brave, passionate, and constant, suffering from
passion as from a disease. His speech is often mere extravagance; but once,
when he waits for Cressida in the orchard,he speaks perhaps the most sensitive
lines in Shakespeare: "I am giddy... The enemy fying"In those lines we
get what is most precise and exquisite in the play,free,for the moment,of all
irony:a rendering of sensation sharpened to the vanishing-point; the sensation
which does not knowitself forpain or pleasure,so inexplicably is it intermingled
in the delights of opposites.Much of what seems to us most characteristically
modern in modern literature,together with almost the whole aim of modern
music,is here anticipated. It is Shakespeare showing us, in a fash, that he
may be quite fair, all of ecstacy that does really exist in the thing he holds up
to our mockery.

167
[6.]
Editor supposes,appears from these considerations,First,If he hadrepresented
himself as running from a falling city,he could never have said,"I have ... ex-
pos'd myself From certain and possess'd conveniences, To doubtful fortunes."
Secondly,The absolute knowledge of the fall of Troy was a secret hid from the
inferior Gods themselves; as appears from the poetical history of that war. .
All that they knew was, that if such and such things happened Troy would
fall.But the secret, that it was absolutely to fall,was known to none.
The sense here given will admit of no dispute amongst those who know how
acceptable a Seer was amongst the Greeks.So.that this Calchas, like a true
priest,if it must needs be so,went where he could exercise his profession with
most advantage. For it being much less common amongst the Greeks than the
Asiatics, there would be there a greater demand for it.——JoENsoN (ed. 176s):
Iam afraid, that after all the learned commentator's efforts to clear the argu-
mentofCalchas,itwill stillappearliable toobjection;nor doI discover more
to be urged in his defence, than that though his skill in divination deterrmined
him to leave Troy, yet that he joined himself to Agamemnon and his army
by unconstrain'd good-will;and though he came as a fugitive escaping from
deserved reward. This argument is not regularly and distinctly deduced, but
this is, I think, the best explication that it will yet admit.-HeArH (Revisal,
1765, p. 499): The words of Calchas will bear no other reasonable sense, than
that he had abandoned Troy,from the foresight he had of the destruction that
hung over it. and would inevitably overwhelm it.The following passage ...
which Mr.Warburton adduces as inconsistent with this interpretation,is a
strong confirmation of the truth of it.The sense is plainly,You may be sure
Ihave the fullest persuasion of the certainty of my prediction,otherwise I
I must still consider as doubtful.-MALoNE (ed. 17go): Mr. Theobald thinks it

after he had said that he knew his country was undone; but there is no incon-
sistency: he had left, from whatever cause, what was dear to him,... and,
having joined and served the Greeks, was entitled to protection and reward.

probably attach to any explanation of the passage that may be given.But it

sell, but to let its value speak for itself." Of course he means that they will

94. excell) WARBURToN (ed. 1747): It is an high absurdity to say, that any
thing can “excell' in the extremity of little; which little, too, is as blank as
nothing. Without doubt Shakespear wrote, “Valour and pride parcell them-
selves in Hector';i.e.divide themselves in Hector in such a manner, that the
one is almost infinite; the other almost nothing.——JonNsoN (ed. 176s): I would
not petulantly object, that excellence may as well be little as absurdity be high,
but to direct the reader's attention rather to sense than words.Shakespeare's
thought is not exactly deduced.
Nicety of expression is not his character.
The meaning is plain, “ Valour,” says Eneas, " is in Hector greater, than valour
in other men, and pride in Hector is less than pride in other men.So that
Hector is distinguished by the excellence of having pride less than other pride,
and valour more than other valour.

40. Oathj The oath was to fight no more against Troy, and to do all that he
could to brisg ie war to an end.On this basis Priam agreed to the marriage
of Polyxena to Achilles; Hecuba was the intermediary in the arrangement.
See Appendix, Pp. 441 ff, 445-46. All this occurred after the death of Hector.
Because ofhis oath,Achilles refused all solicitations to fight,thus throwing the
Greeks into despair and bringing them near to defeat. He was finally aroused
by thebeatingshis Myrmidons received from Troilus and the reproaches of an
unnamed man.

51-53. transformation. .. Cuckolds] THEOBALD (ed. 1733): I understand

main an eternal monumentofhiswife'sinfidelity.Andhow couid thisbebet-
ter done thanby calling him an“obelisque memorial'?of all human edifices the
most durable. And the sentence rises gradually, and properly from a “statue'"
called the primitive statue'... But by the bull is meant Menelaus; which
title Thersites gives him again afterwards-"The cuckold and the cuckold-
maker are at it—The Bull has the game."—HEATE (Revisal, 1765, P. 5o5):
[Supports Theobald's interpretation.]The memorial is called oblique,because
it was only indirectly such,upon the common supposition that both [bull

have informed the reader,how Menelaus could properly be said to be“the

he be a primitive statue before he existed? Mr. Warburton tells us “he stood
as the great archetype of this character."But toexpose the improprietyand
weaknessofthisobservationwouldlead ustoonearthebordersofprofaneness.

V.11. DE SELINcoURT (Oxford Lectures on Poetry, 1934, Pp. 9o92): As pene-
trating in its psychology [as Iv.iv] is the scene where Troilus, in company with
Ulysses,watches Cressidaact outher treachery with Diomed.Nowhere else
shall wefind sovividapicture of the distraughtmind of theidealist confronted
with the damning reality,a reality which with one side of his nature he pas-
sionately rejects,forit shatters toits foundations thewhole fabricofhislife,
andwhichyet hisreasonforces upon him.His emotion is not merely that of
the lover who finds his mistress false, for he has universalized his passion; his
is thebewilderedconfictofonewhoinamomentiscalledupon to surrender
the key-stone of his faith....
His lot is more tragic than Hamlet's,for he has
not Hamlet's power of thought, of finding escape from a shattered faith in in
tellectual speculation.His whole universe is tottering, and as before the con-
summation of his ideal hewas giddy with expectation, so now he reels before
the inexorable cruelty of fact...
He begs for time to readjust himself to the
whole cruel fact,“To make a recordation to my soule Of euery syllable that
here was spoke.'But when he has digested his experience he emerges a
hardened man of the world.Chaucer's broken-hearted lover,in like case,
has laid his life in ruin [v.1720-22]: “But trewely, Criseyde, swete may, Whom
I have ay with al my might y-served, That ye thus doon, I have it nought de-
served.”Despite everything, it is his fate to love her still, the “best of any

v.ii. The main circumstances of this scene are given by Lydgate and
Caxton: Andromache's dream and her desperate attempts to keep Hector at
home, her appeal to Priam ior support, and Hector's anger with her. Sh. uses
Cassandra in place of Hecuba and the sisters of Hector.In both sources the
dream is more specifc than in Sh., namely that Hector is killed in battle.

Cressida..where Andromache, Cassandra, and Priam are trying to dissuade
Hector from taking the field against Achilles, bears so close a resemblance,
especially in the stress laid on dreams and prophecies,to the scenein the Seven
against Thebes where the Chorus are imploring Eteocles not to go out against
Polynices, that it is diffcult to suppose the resemblance is due to mere coinci-
dence.

25. fcaled] MALONE (ed. 179o): “Scaled" means here, dispersed, put to
flight....
.This is proved decisively by the original reading of the quarto,
"scaling,” which was either changed by the poet himself to“scaled"(with the
same sense)orby the editor of thefolio.If thelatterwas the case,it isprob-
able that not being sufficiently acquainted with our authour's manner, who
frequently uses the active for the passive participle,he supposed that the epi-
thetwas merely descriptive of some qualityin the thing described.--[For evi-
dence of the meaning assigned Malone refers to notes in his edition: Vol. I1,
p.72, note 4 (Measure for Measure), and Vol.vIl, p. 148, note 6 (Coriolanus).
But the curious will find all his learning,and much more, gathered in the
little more'). There is no doubt that “to scale' meant to spread, dislodge,
scatter, and it is curious that N.E.D. omits these meanings, although they oc-
curinHolinshedandother examplesofnon-dialectliterature.Mosteditors
changed it into “shoals."RrrsoN (Remarks, 1783, p. 165):“Sculls"and
"shoals'have not only one and the same meaning,but are,actually,or at
least originally, one and the same word. A “scull of herrings" (and it is to
these fish that the speaker alludes),so termed on the coast of Norfolk and
Suffolk, is elsewhere called a " shoal.""

kills at will, can pick and choose.—-[But the CowDEN CLARKEs (ed.1868) inter-

V.vi. CowDEN CLARKE (ed. r868): The nShalespearian style, which
we mentioned...as beingvisible towards theclose of thisplay,is markedly to
be seen in the present speech.Its every line is touched with the stilted stiffness
and fatness that disfigure the diction of the First Part Henry VI ..; the
passages referred to in ... that same play [1.i.r6s-66: "here take my leave, To go
about my preparation'; 11.i.69-7o: "I was employ'd in passing to and fro,
About relieving of the sentinels']; the awkward expression,“Execute your
aims," has similarity of construction with “rive their dangerous artillery"
[rv.ii.2g]; and the two concluding vapidly pompous lines, “Follow me, sirs,""
&c., are not only in startling contrast with the preceding manner of writing in
the present play,but bear so striking a resemblance to passages in the other,
that we almost feel inclined to believe them theproduction of the same hand.
It is as if Shakespeare had derived this incident ... from some hitherto untraced
source,and had left the two brief scenes describingit just as he had found them
originally written.

RelationsbetweenQandF:
KviGHT(ed.[1841]p.74):From whatever secondary source it proceeded,
there can be no doubt that it[Q] was printed from the genuine copy of the
folio... sufficiently show that the original was most accurately printed.The
alterationsofthefolio arenotcorrectionsoferrorsin theoriginai;but,forthe
mostpart,slightchanges ofexpression.Wehavenodoubt thateach textwas
printed from a different but a genuine copy.
CoLLiER (ed.1842,p.6): The quarto of 16o9 was unquestionably the founda-
tion of thetextofthefolio,forinvariousinstances thelatter adopts theliteral
blundersoftheformer:itbesidesintroducesnotafewimportantcorruptions,
for which it is not easy to account, so that the language of Shakespeare, on
thewhole,isperhapsbestrepresentedin the quarto.
[ED.—The differences in opinion here expressed were carried on by subse-
quent editors and scholars, and still persist. VERPLANCk (ed.1847,p.3) agreed
with Knight that F was printed from a different MS.,“probably one which,
havingbeen usedfor the theatricalcopies,hadreceived some correction from
the author himself." HuDsoN (ed. 1854, P. 355) sided with Collier in thinking
thata copy of Qwas“probably"used forF;but the differences between the
besides the quarto." DELrus' opinion (3d ed., 1872, p. 2), as I understand it,
wasthattheFtextis substantiallythatofQ,but showsreworkingby thepoet
andis therefore thelater andbetter text,whatever advantagesQmayhavein
certain passages being laid to the carelessness with which F was printed.]
CLARK and WRiGHT (ed.186s,p.ix):We find in the Folio several passages
essential to the sense of the context which do not exist in the Quarto,and
printer. On the other hand we find some passages in the Quarto, not absolutely
essential to the sense,thoughadecided improvement to itandquite in the
mutilated form.Sometimes thelineswhicharewrongly dividedintheQuarto
are divided properlyin the Folio,and vice versa:in this point,however,the
former is generally more correct than the latter.The two texts differ in many
singlewords:sometimesthedifferenceisclearlyowingtoaclericalor typo
graphical error, but in other cases it appears to result from deliberate correc-
.On the whole we are of opinion that the Quarto was printed from a tran-
script of the author's original MS.; that this MS. was afterwards revised and
slightly alteredby the authorhimself,and thatbefore thefirstFoliowasprinted
from it, it had been tampered with by another hand. Perhaps the corrections
are due to the writer who did not shrink from prefixing to Shakespeare's play
aprologueofhisown.

The manuscript from which the transcriber made his
directions come from? Surely not from Shakspere. Whence then? Evi.
dently from two different manuscripts,neither in the handwriting of the
author,*neither authoritative,one subsequent to the other,and both marked
with stage-directions by persons not thoroughly familiar with the play.In
other words, it is fairly clear that what happened was something like this:
Shakspere's manuscript (A), in a crude state, disfigured with deletions, altera-
tions of his own; subsequently Shakspere revised his manuscript (A), and then
another scribe (C) made another copy, adding his own stage-directions and
making his own mistakes. B's transcript became Bonian and Walley's "copy"
in 16o9, C's became Heminge and Condell's “copy" in 1623. Shakspere's
original manuscript or the licensed prompt-copy had probably gone the.way of
his other manuscripts,most likely in the fire which destroyed the Globe The
atrein1613.
Three alternatives have been proposed: (r) F was set up from a copy of Q
whichhadbeen corrected from a manuscript;(2)Q and F were both set up
from the same MS.,but this MS.had undergone revision between Q and F;
(3) they were set up from different and independent manuscripts.The con-
sensus (Knight, Verplanck, Pollard, Adams, Lee, Greg, Tannenbaum) has been
for the third alternativeWemustrowcaamine at least someof the evidence
onwhichadecisionwillrest.

Peculiarities ofQMS.:
I.There is a notable tendency to substitute afor ein certain words.Thus

2.To substitute e for i-y, as hether and prethee for hither and prythee.
3.MS.o is often read α.Thus ath' several times for o'th'; lad for Lord
(v.i.ss); spartan for sparrow (v.vii.13)。

The spelling peculiarities might be those of the author, of a scribe, or of a
Iincline to believe that theywere,because the hether and swarue groups suggest
aprovincialism of habitwhichaLondon printerwouldnotbelikely toimpose
onhis copybutwhichhemightnotchangeinthe copybeforehim.Thesame
shouldof coursebe saidfor aprofessionalLondon scribe.It couldnotbe

provincial writing habits. There is still the possibility that the peculiarities
are Sh.'s.
Conclusions:
1. F was not set up from Q but from a manuscript.*
2. The MS. for Q was rather hard, in places, to read. The o's which looked
like a's and the a's which looked like u's suggest rapid or careless writing, and
this is also the impression that some of the corruptions in Q give. The MS
forFwas certainly clearer andless subject to misadventure.
3.Fwas not setup from theQMS.,unless one iswilling tobelieve thatin
allplaceswhereFvaries fromQitrepresents Sh.'s lastthoughts.Butno one
seemstobelievethat.InsomeimportantinstancesFisanteriortoQ,not
because its readings are poorer (a matter about which there is always room for
disagreement) but because they are manifestly earlier.Therefore we must
suppose that theoriginal textunderwent some emendmentbeforeit appeared
in print as Q.And F shows clearly that subsequently to the publication of Q
the text had been further emended.Yet F preserves some passages that had
been altered in Q.
4.I see no valid objection to supposing that Q was set from Sh.'s autograph,
althoughIadmitwith Chambers andTannenbaum that the fact cannotbe
proved from the printed text. It is not in any case very important, but it
that this revised copy found its way to Bonian and Walley.But the copy (or
original autograph) which Sh.retained did not have these revisions.Subse-
quently he again and. more thoroughly checked over the play, making some
hundreds of minor changes, a few cuts, a few additions.This copy became
the property of Heminge and Condell, whether directly from Sh. or from some
other party,whether in the originalautograph or not,I should not care to
guess.If anyone should ask me why Sh.did not consult Q to find out what
previous changes he had made I should not know how to answer.I can only
say that my theory (not greatly different from Tannenbaum's) offers a working
hypothesisforresolvingthe complexrelationshipsofthetwotexts.Something
like this must have happened.

FLEAy (On the Composition of Troylus and Cressida,"N.S.S. Trans.1874,
pp. 304-17) proposed three periods of composition. The love story belongs
about 1594(after Romeo and before The Merchant ofVenice);theHector-Ajax
Achilles story of the stratagem tobring Achilles backinto the war(written
after thepublication of Chapman'sHomer,from which Thersites comes)be-
longs about 16o6-o7. The primary guide is style. The love story is akin in
style to Romeo,Richard II,and The Merchant, and the prose of Pandarus is
reminded in its conceits, its dirty jokes, the peculiar turn of its comparisons,
the fow of its metre, the unstayed youthfulness of its ideas, and the sensuous
passionateness of its love—of the companion play of Romeo and Juliet..
Try the experiment; prepare your ear by reading straight off a couple of
Acts of Romeo and Juliet,and then read this Troylus story without a word
of the other parts of the play,asfar asIv.iv,and I confidently await the
verdict..The styleof[the]secondpartismore advanced than thefirst:
butnot somuchsoasmanyof thesecond-periodplays.Itremindsusmostof
the Merchant of Venice or John...In [the third] part, and this only,we
have the style of Shakspere's third-fourth manner in metre;in word-coining;
inmetaphor;indevelopmentofcharacter.Ineednotdwellonthis,itisthe
extreme palpability of this fact that has caused all this play tobe usually as
signed to the date of 16o8, or thereabouts"(pp. 307-io).When checked by
ratios are: for the love story, r:8.4; for the Hector story, 1:13.6; for the
Achillesstory,I:54.5.

BATcHELDER (University of Iowa dissertation, 1938, unpublished; from Con-
clusion): Ir name and general outline the play is an acknowledgment of the
past,but in spirit and in many of its details it is a reflection of the last years of
theElizabethanperiod.Thepoliticalideasofthe Greeks and theTrojans are
frankly modern in their recognitionof theideals andpractices which obtained
in the Tudor state.The factional interests,the undignified squabbles and
jealousies,the slanders,the cunning,and the secret plots of the Greeks belong
to the “Greeks"of Elizabethan political life. Likewise the strong current of
nationalistic feeling, the emphasis upon honor, the magnanimity, and the
candor of the Trojans belong to the Elizabethan “Trojans."The social and
moral atmosphere is that of the Elizabethan court.The conversation, pene
trated with sophisticated wit and colored with subtle and indecent suggestion,
is the conversation of contermporary courtiers and ladies.The islet of virtue
and the surrounding ocean of vice are contemporary. The sensuality of the
women is that of Elizabethan gentlewomen; and the sexual excesses of many
of themen are thoseofElizabethan courtiers.WhateverShakespeareselects
from source or tradition has its close counterpart in contemporary life; and
whatever he contributes is unmistakably Elizabethan.[ED.-Throughout
the dissertation it is strongly suggested,if not affirmed, that the “islet of
virtue”is Hector-Essex,and the“ocean of vice"is Ulysses-Cecil and his clan.

tured the loved one as a marvellous phenomenon, half queen, half gipsy, al-
luring and repellant, true and false, strong and weak, a siren and a mystery;
this is the standpoint of Antony and Cleopatra. Then, possibly, when life had
sobered him down, when he had cooled,as we all do cool in the hardening ice
of experience, he suddenly and sharply realised the insanity of an exotic en-
thusiasm for so worthless an object. He looks upon this condition, which
invariably begins with self-deception and must ofnecessity endin disillusion-
ment, as a disgraceful and tremendous absurdity; and his wrath over wasted
feelings and wasted time and suffering,over the degradation and humiliation
of its self-deception,and ultimately the treason itself, seeks final and supreme
Cpessida.

Troilus is a very hard play to view dispassionately.It has been called the
least Shn.of plays and the one in which the poet seems tobe writing most for
himself.It has been called a marvel of genius and a bad piece of bungling.
If a criticfindsin theplay dissonances which cannot beresolved tohis satis-
faction by such practical explanations as hasty composition, revision of an old
play,obedience to tradition,or distastefor the subject(apoint of Tatlock's
which itself invades the subjective),he must necessarily look for the cause in
the private life of Sh. After all, the poet was presumably not given the sub-
ject,he did not have to write a scathing arraignment of woman's inconstancy.
And although drama is in form and often in fact the most objective of the
written arts,it does not follow that every play is objective,or even every
dramatist-witness Strindberg in our times or Jonson (of Cynthia's Revels and
Poetaster) in Sh.'s. There is nothing in the nature of drama to keep a play
from being full of personal allusions or of personal feelings.The assumption
that Sh.is always the objective artist,the practical man of affairs whose leading
motive was to write successful stage plays,is a wise check to fancy,but it is
onlyapremise,theuniversalvalidityofwhich cannomorebeprovedthan can
is that there are no facts as to Sh.'s own purely subjective personal feelings;
so cannotidentify them in his writings,but must substitute our own,as hewas

VI.SUMMARY
The whole question is not,at bottom,academic but is directly pertinent to
the mystery of Sh.'s creative processes.We know something about Shn.
poetic paraphrase from Holinshed and North's Plutarch,in cases where the
indebtednesscanbefollowedalmostwordforword.Butheretheimplications
arefarmore complex,notablyinGayley'shypothesisofacourseleadingfrom
Homer through Chaucer,Boethius, possibly Elyot,to Hooker;to which Han-
fordwould add,somewhere along theway,Plato.Coleridge'spoetic courses
might be something like that, but were Sh.'s? If he used as much from Hooker
as Gayley finds, it argues a degree of assimilation not supported by the
Holinshed-Plutarch paraphrases,although not on that account impossible.
What should be bornein mind is that the speech ofUlyssesfollows a familiar
pattern, as does the speech of Canterbury in Henry V.The pattern,repeated
in the various political treatises of the age,presents a picture of orderly govern-
ment based on a supreme head and on the harmonious relations of parts,illus-
trated by the similitudes ofmusicalharmony(ExeterinHenry V)or thehive
(Canterbury and Ulysses), followed by one of the chaos which results from
sedition andademocraticdisruptionoforder,oftenillustratedbythefigure of
the human body whose functions refuse to work together (Menenius in Corio-
lanus, 1.i). Order among men is always presented as a part of the law of
nature,corresponding toorder among theheavenlybodiesandtheelements.
Forinstance,wefind this conceptand thebee-similitude on the samepage of
Guillaume de la Perriere's Miroir politique (The Mirror of Policie,1599,
sig.B+v):
himselfe, hath after a sort expressed this royall kind of gouernmet, as wel in
things sensible(though notpartakers of reason)asin things withoutlife:
The Bees being gouerned and pricked forward by an instinct of Nature,
haue one only king, vnder vvhose authority they go to vvarre, dispose of
their affaires,and liue in society togither,acknowledging one king as their
only Generall and Gouernour ...what shall I say more, if we look vp vnto
the heauens, do not vve see one Sunne beare rule and principality ouer the
rest of the starres?"

And the pictures of seditious chaos roughly correspond with that part of

“It [sedition] engendreth and nourisheth want of reverence towards God,
disobedience to Magistrats,corruption of maners,change of laws,contempt
ofjustice,andbase estimation oflearningand sciences.It causethhornible

kinsman against kinsman, men of the same nation, province, and citie, one
againstanother.
In theend,thebodie thus dismembred,and theparts
thereof infected with the same poison of discord,destroy themselves."
It is not necessary, or wise, therefore to suppose, without a more compelling
parallel than we have yet found, that the speech of Ulysses is indebted to any
one treatise, or to any certain group.We may be sure that Sh.was familiar
with some of the standard works on government, and with the rather stereo-
typed order and details of presentation.He follows the pattern,but the em-
broidery we may suppose to be his own, to spring to hand out of his abounding
and pictorial imagination.Yet the possibility must be admitted that he, a
master of words and images, was fred by other masters of words and images,
and that some recollection of Hooker and Spenser,whom he certainly must
have read, directed his choice or colored his language.

B.-FACULTY PSYCHOLOGY IN TROILUS
ANDCRESSIDA
There isconsiderable specificusein TroilusandCressidaof the technical
terms and processes of the faculty psychology of Shakspere's day.As Sir
John Davies (Nosce Teipsum, 1599, Pp. 46-so) explains, the five senses "are
the outwardInstrumentsofSense..Andyet thesePorters whichallthings
admit,Them seluesperceiue not,nor discerne the things:One Commonpower
doth in the forehead sit, Which all their proper formes together brings."
This common power is the Imagination or Common Sense. “This inward
Sense doth absent things retaine; Yet straight transmits all formes she doth
perceiue, Vnto a higher region of the braine. Where Phantasie, neare hand
maid to the mind, Sits, and beholds, and doth discerne them all" Wit
"Lookes in the mirrour of the phantasie, Where all the gatherings of the
Senses are.From thence this power the shapes of things abstracts,And them
acts,And so the formes of single things perceiues.But afterby discoursing
know,And all effectes into their causes brings."

J.F.PALMER(Transactions ofRoyalSoc.ofLit.,2nd Ser.,xV,1893,64ff.):
I have little doubt that Shakespeare was largely indebted for character-
material to the edition [of Homer] published in 1598, in which the Third,
Fourth,Fifth,and Sixth Books were omitted.Of this there is striking evidence
both in the rha-zcters themselves and in the sequence of events in the Play.
The characters of Agamemnon, of Achilles, of Ulysses, of Nestor, and of
Thersites, as well as the quarrel between Agamemnon and Achilles, are all
indicated in the firsttwoBooks oftheIliad.In Troilus and Cressida Shake
speare, having introduced us to these heroes, and shown us the immediate
results of the quarrel, passes on at once in the first Act to the subject-matter
oftheSeventhBook,the challenge ofHector to theGreeks,andits acceptance
by Ajax Telamon, whose character is there indicated. This continues through
There are also allusions to other matters contained in the Seventh Bcok,as
well as to some in theNinth andEleventh,including the embassy toAchilles;
while the Third,Fourth,Fifth,and Sixth Bcoks,which relate the acts of
Diomede, Hector's prophecy,and the wound of Mienelaus, are entirely passed
over.To the duel between Mlenelaus and Paris, there is, perhaps, an indirect
allusion in Act 1, Scene i [rr8]; but that is all. The celebrated speech of
Ulysses in support of military discipline (Act 1, Scene i) is clearly suggested by
that in the Second Book of the Iliad.*..The character of Ajax, again, is

detailsbetweenA and B,and if Coffersnothingwhich is not supplied by B,
then B is the source for A.But he fails to make any examination of Lydgate
tosee if thiscondition istrue.

that isin Lydgate but not in Caxton,but that there is material from Caxton
thatis notin Lydgate.It is allin rv.v,and comprises the following points:in

Calchas; in Caxton and Sh. Hector embraces Ajax after their fight, in Lydgate
Nevertheless,although Caxton seems to have been the main source, in three
instances the correspondence with Lydgate is more extensive and more signif-
cant:(1) the characterization of Troilus (Iv.v.1zr ff.);(2) the episode cf Hector
and the knight in sumptuous armor (v.vi and vi): and (3) the instructions of
Achilles tohis Myrmidons (v.vii).In all three cases itishard not tobelieve
that Lydgate is the source. The reader, however, may judge for himself.↑

The whole character of Pandarus, the middle-aged uncle of Cressida, with
his frequent jests and real affection for both Troilus and Cressida,is taken
directly from Chaucer's“japing”Pandarus.In Caxton's Recuyell not even
the name of Pandarus occurs in connection with the Troilus story;in Lydgate's
Troye-book thename occurs onlyin avery brief summary(33lines)of Chaucer's
story.Both Lydgate and Caxton refer the reader to Chaucer for a full ac
count.
The character of Troilus,too,shows an enthusiastic dreaminesslike that of
Chaucer'syoung lover;this is combined with the stern,warrior-like qualities
corresponding to Caxton'scharacterizationofTroilus.
The incidents of the story, moreover, everywhere show the infuence of
Chaucer's expanded narrative.

I.STRUCTURALANALYSIS
[B.The Elizabethans had evolved a definite system of five-act structure,
which furnishes an objective control for the basicinterpretation of any one of
their plays.* In Troilus, the prologue informs us that the story is of Troy;
Troilus and Cressida are not even mentioned.Then in Act 1,↑ in balanced
form, the dramatist has introduced the Trojans in their city,and the Greeks
upon the plain,balanced as in the prologue and throughout the play.He has
chosen to use the infatuation of Troilus for Cressida,rather than that of Paris
for Helen, upon which to string his introductory Trojan scenes. Then the
disruptive rivalry of Achilles and Ajax portrays the Greek situation. And
this has been given the pride of place at the end of the first act,where the prob-
lem of theplay mustbe exhibited.

functions of a second act, so as to occasion thebeginning of the epitasis in the
third.Again,as in the frst act, the pride of place at the end of the act has
beengiven totheplotofUlyssestoforceAchilleseventuallyinto thefight

TATLocR's reconstruction (P.M.L.A., xxx, 1915, 697-7o2) is briefly as follows:
Scene 1: “... clearly the council-scene, found in all versions, in which Priam
consultswith his sons and chiefcounsellors as to whether they are toreturn
Helen.The presence of Priam and Cassandra proves the scene to be in Troy;
theheralds and tuckets indicate an embassy;the presence of Ulysses and
Diomed suggests that its purpose was to demand the return of Helen ... the
entrance of Cassandra at the end can only be to lament their fatal decision."'

HEYWOOD'S IRON AGE, Pt. I
Whateverrelation may existbetween thefirstpart of ThomasHeywood's
Iron Age and Sh.'s Troilus involves the question of priority. FLEAy (Bio-
graphical Chronicle,1891,I,283-85)had dated all the Age plays of Heywood
between 1595 and 1597. TATLocK (P.M.L.A., xxx, 1915, 706-718) argued
for 1594-96,making a special point that The Iron Age must have preceded
Heywood's Troia Britannica (the Stationers'Register,5 Dec.,16o8; published
16o9),not followed it. But with respect to Fleay's dating, and by inference
to Tatlock's, CLARK (1931, p. 63) says:“The evidence in refutation of this
theory is so overwhelming that we are forced simply to assert here that The
Ages are,beyond the shadow of a doubt, dramatizations of Heywood's own
Troia Britannica." And CHAMBERs (Wm. Sh., 193o, I, 449, with specifc
clear inference from the epistles to Heywood's earlier Ages that the Iron Age,
in r611,although it was contemplated‘by God’s grace'in 16r3.And I think
we must ascribe the paralleis with Troilus and Cressida to borrowings by
Heywood from Shakespeare."Tatlock,however,had not expressed the opin-
ion that Sh. borrowed from Heywood-he had merely said that if one play
owed anything to theother the debtwasSh.'s.Hisown theorywas thatboth
plays made use of the same antecedent play. But since (p. 755, n.62) he
cannot find that antecedent in the Admiral's fragment (which lacks Thersites
and theduelbetweenHectorandAjax)norintheDekker-Chettleplay(ifthat
be identified with the Admiral's fragment), the source-play becomes a very
lostplayindeed.
Comparisonoftheextractsprintedhereafterfrom theIronAgewithTroilus
shows that resemblances are few and with one exception not in any way re-
markable.Episodes common tobothplays are:the single combatbetween
Hector and Ajax;theattemptofAndromache,Priam,and Hecuba to dissuade
Hectorfrombattle;Thersites'exhibition of cowardice on thebattlefeld;and
Achilles' use of his Myrmidons in killing Hector. The frst two are in Hey-
wood's source, Caxton's Recuyell,and owe very little in their treatment to
Sh.; the last two are not and may have been suggested by Troilus. There are
two or three cases of resemblance in expression,pointed out in footnotes.But
themoststrikingof these,Hector's division ofAjaxintohis Trojan andGreek
halves,loses some ofitsforceinview ofthefactthatthe same thought occurs
in Marston (see note on Troilus, Iv.v.i42). On the whole, the impression one
getsis ofapparentpains taken to avoid duplication.Surely the onlyreason
for treating the Troilus-Cressida story so scantly, without a single echo of Sh.,
is that it had been fully treated already.The one real exception to this evi-
dently intentional divergence is the figure of Thersites.Even he is made as
unlike Sh.'s Thersites as two snarling cynics can be, but yet the fact remains
that a feeting personality of the Iliad is elevated into a main character.
Either that is a deliberate imitation of Sh., or else both characters are imitations
conceptofThersitesatthetime.)

concludes concerning the ages,“Perhaps composition of the dramas came

Age.Sometime during the process, or perhaps a little later, he remembered

But obviously his plan calledfor completion of theseries.
In fishing his task, he found the old Troy useful, and also, in a limited way,

JustasHeywoodseemstohaveavoidedduplicationinscenario,soheseems
tohave avoided it in characterization.Many ofhis people,like Troilus and
Cressida,have no character.But his Ajax and his Paris are very unlike the
Ajax and Paris of Sh.,and his Achilles,although he shares traits ofpride and
treachery,is on the whole a quite differentAchilles.And above all,there is
noneofthedenigrationoftheGreeksandpartialityfor theTrojanswhichone
finds in Sh. Achilles, Ajax, and Diomed are the three heroes of Greece, bal.
anced by Hector, Troilus, and Paris of Troy.In prowess, chivalry,manners,
and faults they are pretty nearly even. The treachery of Achilles in killing
Hector is matched by the treachery of Paris in killing Achilles.Iam quite
good corrective for those whoare unduly impressed by the singularity of
Troilus,I should say thatno better measure could be found for the remarkable
originality and differentness of Troilus.In intellect,artistry,and purpose the
twoplays are about as much alike as anaive child and amature man.

LATERSTAGEHISTORY
DRYDEN
Dryden's Troilus and Cressida was produced at Dorset Garden about April,
1679 (N1coLL, 1923, P. 36o), with Betterton as Troilus, Leigh as Pandarus,
Underhill as Thersites, Mrs. Mary Lee as Cressida, and Mrs. Betterton as
Andromache. It was published in 1679 and again in 1695.
DRyDeN, Preface* to Troilus and Cressida:For the play itself, the author
[Sh.] seems to have begun it with some fire; the characters of Pandarus and
Thersites are promising enough; but as if he grew weary of his task, after an
entrance or two, he lets them fall: and the latter part of the tragedy is nothing
but a confusion of drums and trumpets, excursions and alarms. The chief
persons, who give name to the tragedy, are left alive; Cressida is false, and is
not punished. Yet, after all, because the play was Shakespeare's, and that
there appeared in some places of it the admirable genius of the author,I under-
wholly buried. Accordingly, I new-modelled the plot, threw out many un-
necessary persons, improved those characters which were begun and left un-
finished,as Hector, Troilus, Pandarus, and Thersites,and added that of
Andromache.After this,I made,with no small trouble,an order and con-
nection of all the scenes; removing them from the places where they were
I have so ordered them, that there is a coherence of them with one another, and
a dependence onthemain design;noleaping fromTroy to theGrecian tents,
and thence back again, in the same act, but a due proportion of time allowed
for every motion.I need not say that I have refined his language, which
before was obsolete;but I am willing to acknowledge,that as Ihave often
drawn his Englishnearer to our times,so I have sometimes conformed my
own to his; and consequently, the language is not altogether so pure as it is
significant.The scenes of Pandarus and Cressida,of Troilus and Pandarus,
of Andromache with Hector and the Trojans, in the second act,are wholly
new; together with that of Nestor and Ulysses with Thersites, and that of
Thersites with Ajax and Achilles.I will not weary my reader with the scenes
which are added of Pandarus and thelovers,in the third,and those of Ther-
sites,which are wholly altered;butI cannot omit the last scene in it,which is
almost half the act,betwixt Troilus and Hector.The occasion of raising it
washinted to mebyMr.Betterton;the contrivanceandworking ofitwas my
own。
They who think to do me an injury by saying that it is an imitation of
the scene betwixt Brutus and Cassius, do me an honour by supposing I could
imitate the incomparable Shakespeare; but let me add, that if Shakespeare's
Tragedyl,had never been,yet Euripides had furnished me with an excellent
thence,indeed,the last turn of it is borrowed.The occasion which Shake-

Dryden (1882,VI,255-391).

A Camp. Enter AGAMEMNON, ULysSEs, DIOMEDES,and NESTOR.
Agam. Princes, it seems not strange to us, nor new,
That, after nine years' siege, Troy makes defence,
Sinceeveryactionofrecordedfame
Has withlongdifficultiesbeeninvolved,
Notanswering thatidea of the thought,
Which gave it birth;why then,you Grecian chiefs,
With sickly eyes do you behold our labours,
Andthinkthemourdishonour,whichindeed
Are the protractive trials of the gods,
Toproveheroic constancy inmen?
Nest. With due observance of thy sovereign seat,
GreatAgamemnon,Nestor shall apply
Thy well-weighed words.In struggling with misfortunes
Lies the true proof of virtue: On smooth seas,
How many bauble-boats dare set their sails,
And makean equalway with firmervessels!
Butlet thetempestonce enrage that sea,
And then behold the strong-ribbed argosy,
Boundingbetween the ocean and theair,
Like Perseus mounted on his Pegasus.
Then where are thoseweakrivaisofthemain?
Or, to avoid the tempest, fed to port,
Or made a prey to Neptune.Even thus
Do empty show,andtrue-prizedworth,divide
In storms of fortune.

Ulys. Mighty Agamemnon!
Heart of our body, soul of our designs,
In whom the tempers,and the minds of all
Should be enclosed,—-hear what Ulysses speaks.

Ulys.Troyhadbeendown ere this,andHector's sword
Wanted a master, but for our disorders:
The observance due to rule has been neglected.
Observe how many Grecian tents stand void
Upon this plain, so many hollow factions:
For, when the general is not like the hive,
To whom the foragers should all repair,
What honey can our empty combs expect?
Or when supremacy of kings is shaken,
What can succeed? How could communities,
Or peaceful traffc from divided shores,
Prerogative of age, crowns, sceptres, laurels,
But by degree, stand on their solid base?
Then everythingresolves to brutalforce,
And headlong force is led by hoodwinked will.
For wild ambition,like a ravenous wolf,
Spurred on by will, and seconded by power,
Must make an universal prey of all,
And last devouritself.
Nest. Most prudently Ulysses has discovered
The maladywhereof our state is sick.
Diom. 'Tis truth he speaks; the generai's disdained
By him one step beneath,he by the next;
Thatnextbyhimbelow:Soeach degree
Spurns upward at superior eminence.
Thus our distempers are their sole support;
Troy in our weakness lives, not in her strength.

H. SpENcER (1g27, Pp. 231-32): Concerning the play as a whole I venture
the opinion that structurally it is superior to Shakespeare's.This conclusion
is not based on Dryden's ingenious jig-sawing of the Trojan and Grecian scenes
andhis dovetailingofthemsothathegives usbut sixshiftsbetween city and
camp, while Shakespeare gives us nine; nine changes are no more confusing
than six.But at two points Dryden has grasped a situation that Shakespeare
failed to grasp,and has exploited it to not only theatric but genuine dramatic
advantage.These situations are,first, Troilus's reception of the news that
Cressida must leave Troy; and second, the ending of the play.In the hands
ofa sweet and dignified Cressida,an accomplished tragedian as Troilus,and a
coollyinsolent stagevillain asDiomedes,thefinal scenemusthave acted ad
mirably. If I were an actor, I wouid rather play Dryden's Troilus than
Shakespeare's. Cressida, however, is another story. Like Cleopatra she has
lost variety; she is neither a lazar kite nor a natural coquette, but simply
Woman in Love. Yet, once granted this conception of her character, Dryden
writeswellforher.

attention wrongly.In structure,Shakespeare's Troilus was the play most in
even with modern Shakespearean staging, and Dryden did well to try to unify
it.But the ethical assumptions and theview of human nature which underlay

understand. To the theme of political order, he gives something of his own

intellectual, object of the play is perfectly clear, ...‘You glorify war? I will

Ajax thebooby and Diomed thecheat...
 I mock at honor in war; purity in

(RobertFletcherde-
signed)a workable set which would permit rapid and continuous action
and a minimum of changes.He devised a framework with supports which
framed the inner stage, and on the framework hung curtains which could be
tent or Pandarus'house,drawn aside partially or altogether when exterior
action required. Simple properties, suggestive rather than literal, gave the
illusion of the Greek camp and of Diomed's tent outside which Troilus listens
to Cressida's betrayal. For the brief transitional scenes a curtain was drawn
across the forestage, and for the battle at the end the ground was cleared
as much as possible topermit maximummovement and minimum of stumbling
over needless obstacles.Clever lighting helped differentiate between exterior
andinterior scenes andwasemployed throughout asanintegralpartof the
story,not for the purpose of startiing the audience with unusual effects.
The constuming, by no means literally classical. had a quality that com-
bined thepictorial with the satiric moodof the text.Cressida's robes were
feminine and revealing, enhancing the girl's beauty but indicating also the
something less than modest aspect of her nature. Patroclus and Pandarus,
.with whom the text is so unsparing,proclaimed their effeminate and degenerate
attributes by their dress,while the kings and warriors were imposing;and,
when the occasion called for it, grandiose and even a little absurd. .. The
audience on opening night was interested but startled to observe that Greeks
and Trojans alike were wearing curious wire frameworks on their heads in
place of helmets...
Commentingfavorablyon thiscleverdevicetooneof

prove his thesis.His version goes as follows:
I.i-ii: unchanged.
1.ii: based on Iliad, Bk. ii. There is mutiny in the Greek camp; most of
for the disaffected and is beaten by Ulysses,who strives vainly to check the
revolt.Agamermnon yields unwillingly to the crowd and sends Nestor with
an offer ofpeace if Helen is returned.Aeneas arriveswith Hector's challenge.
Ulysses proposes to Agamemnon the plan of stirring up Achilles by promoting
Ajax.In this scene and elsewhere Nestor is much reduced and the leadership
of Ulysses is emphasized.
.i--i: unchanged.
I1.ii:somewhat curtailedatthe end.
Il.i:unchanged exceptfor the addition of a chorus.
Il.ii-ii,Iv.i: essentially as in Sh.,with minor changes in m.ii.
Iv.ii-iv:combined but unchanged become Iv.ii.
IV.v becomes Iv.i: considerably rearranged, and Cressida is omitted. Here
and elsewhere Achilles is treated more sympathetically than by Sh., and Ajax
is a mere ass.

DRAKE (1817, II1, 439-4o): The play is, indeed, a most perfect unique both
in its construction and effect, appearing to be a continued sarcasm on the tale
of Troy divine, an ironical copy,as it were, of the great Homeric picture.
Whether this was in the contemplation of Shakspeare, or whether it might
not,inagreatmeasure,fowfrom thenature of the Gothicnarratives to which
he had recourse, may admit of some doubt. As Homer, however, was in part
before him, in the excellent version of Chapman, it appears to us, that it cer-
tainly was his design to expose the follies and absurdities of the Trojan war;
the despicable nature of its origin, and the furious discords which protracted
its issue.In doing thishehas stripped theHomericcharacters of all theirepic
pomp; he has laid them naked to the very heart, but he has, at the same time,
individualised them, with a pencil so keen, powerful, and discriminating, that
we become more intimately acquainted with them, as mere men, from the
perusal of this play, than from all the splendid descriptions of the Greek poet.

MATTHEws (1913, P. 233): Although the play is without any possible popu-
larity on the stage, it is not without qualities which demand consideration in
the study.It is unworthy of Shakespeare as a playwright, but it sometimes
heightens our opinion of him as a poet and as a philosopher. Even more does it
disclose his power as a psychologist. He has here given us a group of unheroic
and unlovely characters, marvelously etched, bitten into the plate by the acid
of his satire. Never in any of his plays did he create a character more evil-
mouthed than Thersites,and hardlyever did he create acharacter more con-
sistent and more convincing. Thersites is incessant in railing; he is full of all
manner of uncharitableness,boiling over with envy,hatred and malice; he is a
common scold whose tongue is against every man; he is mean and malignant,
voiding his venom on humanity at large.This vituperative and vitriolic per-
sonality is alive in every utterance, with an appalling vitality;and his temper
is a forerunner of that which we find more than once in Swift, whom Shak-
spere here anticipates, as he anticipated so many other of the authors who
weretocomeafterhim.

characters of his personages were already outlined-so lost his personal con-
sciousness in the individuality of his own creations that they think and feel as

says thus and so; for it is not Shakespeare who speaks, but they with his lips.
